summary: The How many tables calculator works out number of seats at one table from the space for one person at the table, the length and the radius. Think of it as a shortcut for a practical question that turns up in daily life. The unit chips sit next to the boxes, which is where most hand-calculation mistakes start.

sections.title: How does the How many tables calculator work?
sections.html:
The How many tables calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports number of seats at one table in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the table shape); then you type in the space for one person at the table, the space for one person at the table (2), the length (b) and the radius (r).

Press Calculate and the page works through the equation with the values you supplied and derives the rest; it then keeps up with you as you correct a typo.

sections.title: The formula behind the How many tables calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Number of seats at one table=2 × rounded down, (length (b) ÷ space for one person at the table)
Number of seats at one table=rounded down, (2 × PI × radius (r) ÷ space for one person at the table)
How many tables I need=(rounded up, ((1 ÷ 2) × total number of guests ÷ rounded down, (length (b) ÷ space for one person at the table)))
How many tables I need=(rounded up, (total number of guests ÷ rounded down, (2 × PI × radius (r) ÷ space for one person at the table)))

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Suppose I want to know set to How many people I can seat at my table, Table shape set to Rectangular, Space for one person at the table = 30 cm and Length (b) = 30 cm. Working through the relationship above gives Number of seats at one table = 2 and How many tables I need = 5.

Read it as a template. Every number above can be replaced with one of yours; only the relationship between them is fixed.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Number of seats at one table = 2 and How many tables I need = 5 should be roughly the size you expected from I want to know set to How many people I can seat at my table and Table shape set to Rectangular.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

Display rounding is separate from calculation rounding: the digits you see are shortened, the value behind them is not. Numbers far from everyday size are shown in scientific notation so the significant digits stay readable.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The How many tables calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Checking a figure someone else quoted
  • Testing how sensitive an answer is to one input
  • Turning a rough idea into a number you can act on
  • Any time the same 3 figures keep coming back — the space for one person at the table, the length and the radius — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.
  • Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.

faq.q: What does the How many tables calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns number of seats at one table, derived from the space for one person at the table, the length and the radius. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the How many tables calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the space for one person at the table, the length and the radius, which is 7 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter space for one person at the table in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Space for one person at the table opens in centimeters and the chip beside it offers 34 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There are several choices to make (2 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Number of seats at one table = 2. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the How many tables calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
